claims.sentence: In the UK propranolol is available on prescription only, and is made as tablets, slow-release capsules and a liquid.
Propranolol slows the heart rate.
The NHS says it usually starts to work within a few hours.
For heart conditions or high blood pressure the full effect can take 2 to 3 weeks.
For migraine prevention it can take several weeks to make a real difference, so the benefit is not immediate.
The NHS says the most common side effects are usually mild and do not last long.
These are feeling dizzy or tired, cold hands or feet, difficulty sleeping and nightmares.
Dizziness is most likely when first starting or after an increase in dose, and the NHS says anyone affected should not drive, ride a bike or use tools or machinery.
Hospital leaflets also list nausea and diarrhoea or constipation.
The NHS describes serious side effects as rare.
It advises contacting a doctor or NHS 111 straight away for unusual or easy bruising.

The NHS lists several situations where propranolol may not be suitable, including a past allergic reaction to it or another medicine, low blood pressure, a slow heart rate, worsening heart failure, and lung disease or asthma.
UK patient leaflets say that people who have ever had asthma or wheezing should not take propranolol tablets.
The NHS lists diabetes among the conditions to mention to the doctor, and says propranolol may make it more difficult to recognise the warning signs of low blood sugar.
Leaflets say it may delay the response to treatment of low blood sugar.
On pregnancy, the NHS says propranolol can be taken but may sometimes affect a baby's growth, so extra growth scans are usually offered from around 32 weeks.
The NHS says breastfeeding is acceptable if the baby is healthy, because only tiny amounts pass into breast milk.
Some NHS trust migraine guidance, including from Cambridge University Hospitals, does not recommend it in pregnancy, when planning a pregnancy or during breastfeeding.
